data.title: Obama scathes Trump administration in quippy Ohio campaign rally speech
data.description:
President Obama delivered a harsh assessment Saturday of the Trump administration while rallying supporters for Ohio Democratic midterm candidates former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) and Amy Acton.

The former president directly addressed Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial attack ad featuring his opponent Acton’s estranged mother, his opponent. President Trump and Vice President Vance were among those who defended the commercial, which garnered widespread bipartisan backlash.

“There’s a decency that we should expect out of our public officials. And I don’t know what’s happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody could run an ad like that,” Obama said of the ad. “No office is worth stooping that low.”

In a speech full of quips and punchlines, Obama blasted Trump’s policies and cabinet officials while also taking shots at Republican candidates.

He singled out Trump’s original 2016 message to “drain the swamp,” a call to shake up the Washington establishment.

“Remember that whole thing about drain the swamp? The only thing that got drained was the Reflecting Pool in the National Mall after some no-bid contract got it all messed up,” Obama said.

Obama added he sees Trump as more focused on renovating the White House than on the issues voters care about.

“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama said. “What’s with the gold? … He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

The former president also threw out an insult at Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a frequent target of Democrats over his handling of the Iran war and his “warriors” not “weirdos” rhetoric. Hegseth has called the military “low-T” and mandated testosterone screenings for male service members under 30.

“You’ve got the defense secretary … he’s very focused on important matters like the jawlines and testosterone levels of our troops,” Obama said. “How much time do you think this defense secretary spends looking at himself in the mirror in the morning?”

And, as cost of living remains a major concern for voters, Obama moved on to criticize Trump’s tariff agenda — specifically his trade war with Canada.

“The big trade war he’s started now is with that well-known evil empire, Canada,” Obama said. “I mean these are the people who gave us maple syrup and Martin Short.”

The White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment on Obama’s remarks.

Obama was the last Democrat running for president to win Ohio, and the party has not fared well in the Buckeye State since. The last time a Democrat other than Brown won a Senate race in Ohio was 1992, a fact which would remain true even if he returns to the Senate come November. The state has not elected a Democratic governor since 2006.

A Bowling Green State University poll released last week found Obama was the only public official to have a positive favorability rating among Ohio voters.

data.title: Pentagon drafts Iran attack plans as Tehran threatens aggressive retaliation
data.description:
The U.S. military has drawn up options to potentially attack Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, possibly renewing the conflict that has lasted over eight months. 

The U.S. Central Command (Centcom), which oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East, has plans ready to conduct follow-up strikes against Iran if there’s authorization from the White House, a source aware of the plans, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told The Hill. 

Centcom has a number of strike options in place, which are presented to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, another source aware of the planning said. 

President Trump will leave all of his options open until he has to make the final decision, this source, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, said.

“To me, it looks pretty likely that the U.S. goes back to military strikes on Iran once the midterm elections are passed,” Gregory Brew, an Iran expert at Eurasia Group, said in a Friday interview with The Hill. 

Harrison Mann, a former executive officer of the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) Middle East/​Africa Regional Center, said there are two forms of escalation Trump’s could exercise if he chooses to hit Iran: return to attacking Iranian military and political targets inland or targeting civilian and energy infrastructure if the Israeli military is involved.  

“I emphasize inland because since April, the U.S. has basically not attacked anything except for targets on Iran’s coasts. It has apparently not flown aircraft except for maybe one or two strikes over Iranian territory,” Mann said in a Friday interview with The Hill. “That was probably both to reduce the risk of escalation and because they were not willing to risk having more planes shot down.” 

“The other path; these are not mutually exclusive, and which becomes more likely if Israeli forces are involved would be going directly targeting civilian infrastructure, energy infrastructure, or as we saw the Israelis do at the start of the conflict, universities, police stations, other civilian stuff,” Mann continued. 

When asking the Defense Department for a comment, a Pentagon official said the department’s “job is to develop and present military options to the President.”  

“We don’t speculate on hypothetical situations or future operations,” the official said. 

Centcom did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment. 

The appetite for authorizing kinetic actions comes as the U.S. government looks to pull major concessions from the Islamic Republic amid stalled diplomatic negotiations. Trump himself has warned the U.S. could attack Tehran following the November midterms, where Republicans are fighting to retain both chambers of Congress. 

The Trump administration sees Iran’s economy getting weaker by the day, with the combination of sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade degrading the country’s economy, where inflation is rising. 

“Basically, using force to add to the existing pressures that are on Iran, force them to capitulate, reach a deal, and allow the U.S. to exit the war,” Brew said, adding that part of why the U.S. is considering military strikes is “frustration” with the lack of progress on the diplomatic front. 

“The Iranians are not bending; they’re not showing any flexibility,” he said. “They have a negotiating position that they’ve been sticking to now for several weeks.” 

On Monday, Hegseth visited U.S. troops in the Middle East along with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel.

“We’ve worked with the Israeli military quite a bit. That’s nothing new. We have for a long time. They have great capabilities, and we appreciate their contributions to assuring Iran never gets a nuclear weapon,” Hegseth told reporters on Tuesday in Wisconsin, praising Israel as “good partners.” 

Some regional analysts question if another U.S.-Israel strike campaign — which contributed to the depletion of the Pentagon arsenal of missile interceptors and some exquisite offensive systems, spiked gas prices and rocked the Middle East — would force the Iranian leadership to make concessions. 

“There’s no level of U.S. or Israeli strikes that is going to compel Iran to change course at this point. Iranian leaders not only saw themselves in a fight for personal survival and survival of their regime,” Mann, a former Army major, said. “They’ve increasingly come to understand that they have leverage, they have the upper hand, and they want to drive that advantage to try and get concessions from Trump.

“I think we have already seen quite clearly what the limits are of U.S. and Israeli strikes,” he continued. “It could not destroy Iran’s military capacity, could not destroy its political leadership, even though it assassinated key members.

During the active stage of the war, the U.S. and Israeli militaries destroyed and damaged Iranian launchers and missile magazines. Last month, the Pentagon said the U.S. military destroyed upwards of 90 percent of Iranian ballistic missiles, naval industrial base and drones. 

Trump has previously pulled back from greenlighting kinetic strikes against Iran after the Pentagon would prepare a strike package. 

The U.S. military currently has over 50,000 service members in the Middle East and about 20 warships, some of which are helping enforce the naval blockade in the Arabian Sea. 

There are two aircraft carrier strike groups in the Middle East and a third one, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, is going to the Centcom region to possibly relieve the USS George Washington.  

The Pentagon dispatched 4,000 Marines and sailors aboard three warships, led by USS Makin Island, a Wasp-class amphibious assault ship, to the Middle East as part of the amphibious readiness group. 

The additional battleships and personnel could provide the president with greater options for amphibious landings and other operations. 

Trump has also telegraphed that the U.S. military could strike Pickaxe Mountain, located near the damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility in the Zagros Mountains. But some experts have argued the facility’s depth could mean that the U.S.’s most powerful bunker-buster bombs are not likely to penetrate it, as the site is buried up to 2,000 feet below granite. 

On Wednesday, the State Department ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government employees and their family members from Saudi Arabia as the Iran-backed Houthis continue to attack the Kingdom. 


U.S. intelligence found that Iranian plots to target and kill U.S. officials in the Middle East have “substantially increased,” with efforts reaching “advanced stages,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Secretary of State Marco Rubio. 

“Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel,” Clayton said in a memo to Rubio, who also serves as Trump’s national security adviser. “The lethal plotting efforts by Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries.”

Iranian leaders have signaled privately and publicly that the retaliation in the event of U.S. or Israeli attacks is going to be “bigger,” “more aggressive” and “different” than earlier this year, Brew said. 

Tehran is threatening to hit U.S. bases, warships, oil pipelines, refineries and U.S. allies in the Gulf, as Iran still has drone and missile capabilities.

The potential for renewed hostilities in the region, which was reported earlier by The New York Times, also comes as oil prices reached their highest point since May.

The potential for renewed hostilities in the region also comes as oil prices reached their highest point since May. 

Brent crude oil surpassed $117 a barrel on Friday, while U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate traded around $102. 

“In particular, regional officials and leadership members have been explicitly saying that undersea cables in the Persian Gulf, AI data centers and tech-related infrastructure, all of these will be regarded as targets to be fired on in an event that Iran comes under attack,” Brew noted.

Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and Trump’s special envoy for Syria and Iraq, indicated there could be military action against Iran over the weekend. 

“Could there be a strike this weekend? Absolutely. The president has been clear, I’m giving you American policy, the president is very clear: he’s open, and available and accessible to a deal.  And we’ve been at the table for months and months and months,” Barrack said in an interview with Lebanese-Australian entrepreneur and political commentator Mario Nawfal, which was published on Friday. 

“That was my ambassador…he is a pretty powerful man, I guess,” Trump said when asked about Barrack’s comments on Friday, glancing over to Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R). “If that’s the case, I don’t know anything about it.”

“We may do another little epic fury. Or they’ll agree. If they’re smart, they’ll just say ‘Let’s get down to business.’ I doubt they’ll do that because perhaps they are not smart,” Trump said during his Friday rally in Fort Myers, Fla.

When asked the White House about the Iran strike plans, the office referred The Hill to the president’s gaggle on Friday. 

Trump said on Wednesday the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran and left the door open for kinetic action to resume. 

“We are going to have something one way or the other that’ll happen fairly soon. Most people seem to think it’s after the election, and we’re going to see what happens,” the president told reporters. “But I will say this: what we’ve done with Iran is amazing.”

data.title: Sunday shows preview: Trump's DOJ keeps close eye on election results; Last-minute campaigning heats up
data.description:
With less than two weeks to go before the midterms, the Trump administration is ramping up its warnings about voter fraud and is not ruling out the prospect of weighing in on states’ election certification efforts.

The Justice Department (DOJ) reportedly sent letters Friday to California election officials, directing them to identify potential noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls or “risk significant federal scrutiny.” 

This move followed the DOJ’s lawsuit filed last week against California after state and local officials refused to cross-reference 20,000 names on its voter rolls with a list of individuals the Department of Homeland Security flagged over citizenship status concerns.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) accused President Trump at a campaign event in New Hampshire on Sunday of “trying to quite literally rig the election.”

“He’s trying to get our voting rolls,” he said. “You can’t make this stuff up.”  

On Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche did not rule out intervening in states’ midterm election certification processes, citing the need to do so in a potential “doomsday scenario” when reporters asked him about the matter.

The attorney general added the DOJ has no intention “to improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process.” 

A day later, the DOJ sued to block Alaska from verifying its election results, arguing the fact two candidates in the state’s Senate race share the same name could taint the results. Democrats were quick to slam this move as an attempt from the Trump administration to control the outcome of the competition between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D).

Blanche will join CBS News’s “Face the Nation” and CNN “State of the Union” Sunday, while California Sen. Adam Schiff (D) will appear on NBC News’s “Meet the Press.”

Decision Desk HQ, a nonpartisan election handicapper, gives Democrats an 80 percent chance of retaking control of the House this November as of Saturday. But it predicts a tighter fight for the Senate, with DDHQ giving the party having a 56 percent likelihood of gaining the majority in the upper chamber.

Democrats are already putting plans in place for their anticipated takeover of Congress and weighing how they would confront the Trump administration if given back the majority. 

Trump told reporters Friday he would “veto everything” if the Democrats regained control of the legislature. 

“You veto, veto, veto, and then they come and they say, ‘How do we get it done?’ And you make a deal,” the president said. 

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who has signaled he would not step down from leading Republicans in the lower chamber should his party lose its majority, will appear on Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday.”

Several candidates running in closely watched battleground midterm races are also expected to make an appearance on Sunday broadcasts. 

Iowa Senate candidates Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) will both appear on ABC News’s “This Week” on Sunday. GOP Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers will join “Meet the Press,” while Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D), will appear on “Face the Nation.”

Though Ohio’s gubernatorial candidates are not slated to appear on any Sunday talk shows, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial campaign ad featuring Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s mother may also pop up as a topic of conversation on these broadcasts — as the commercial sparked a media firestorm throughout the week.

DDHQ lists the race between Ramaswamy and Acton as leaning in the Democrat’s favor by around four points. The Ohio Senate race places former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, around the same distance ahead of Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted.

Fuel shortages brought on by the ongoing Iran war continue to strain global energy supplies and ramp up pressure on the Trump administration to address rising costs at the pump ahead of the midterm elections. 

On Thursday, the president signed an executive order aimed at lowering mortgage payments amid rising borrowing costs. 

The order directs the Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte to form a pilot program to cancel insurance premiums for government-backed mortgages once a borrower meets certain requirements. It also establishes a task force to lower home construction costs. 

Additionally, the White House announced Friday it was lifting tariffs on certain Canadian goods after these economic policies faced bipartisan criticism ahead of Nov. 3. 

The New York Times reported Wednesday American and Israeli militaries had developed plans for strikes after the midterm elections. The two countries launched initial strikes in this conflict on Feb. 28. Meanwhile, a Friday U.S. intelligence memo signaled Iranian plots to attack and kill Americans abroad had reached “advanced stages.”

In other international news, Ukrainian officials announced Saturday Starshield satellite services were back up to normal speeds in the country after a controversial slowdown, reportedly ordered by billionaire tech mogul Elon Musk, impacted their defense systems against Russia. 

In a statement shared on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked “all Americans” and partners, such as Congress, the State Department and Trump. 

“The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelensky said. “The restoration began overnight, and by this morning, speeds were already sufficient. This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered ‘shaheds.’”

Earlier this week, Russia indicated it was open to resuming trilateral negotiations with Kyiv and Washington. The White House also announced Friday first lady Melania Trump had secured a localized ceasefire deal in a city on the Russia-Ukraine border. 

Fox News’s senior strategic analyst, retired Gen. Jack Keane, will appear on the network’s “Sunday Morning Futures.”

See the full list of guests on the Sunday morning news shows below:

NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday”: Texas Libertarian Senate candidate Ted Brown, political commentator George Will

CBS News’s “Face the Nation”: Attorney General Todd Blanche, Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D)

CNN’s “State of the Union”: Attorney General Todd Blanche, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens (D)

Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday”: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), former Louisiana Lt. Gov. Mitch Landrieu (D)

NBC News’s “Meet the Press”: Steve Kornacki, Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D)

Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures”: Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.), retired Gen. Jack Keane

ABC News’s “This Week”: Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek (D), Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D)

data.title: Obama endorses Nixon, Jolly in last-minute campaign boost
data.description:
Former President Obama has endorsed the Democratic candidates in Florida’s Senate and gubernatorial races less than two weeks ahead of the midterm elections.

Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Jolly and Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon both shared videos of Obama showing support for their campaigns Saturday morning on social platform X.  

“Real change starts when regular folks stand up for what’s right and Angie has spent her career standing up for you,” Obama, who won Florida in both his presidential campaigns, said in a video shared by Nixon in her post.

In the video, Obama said that Nixon has consistently fought for policies to help people including $15 minimum wage and trying to stop congressional redistricting in Florida.

“One leader willing to stand up again and again for what’s right,” he said. “That’s why I believe Angie will be an outstanding U.S. Senator.”

Nixon said in her post that both her and Obama started as organizers in their communities “because we immediately understood that real changes come from regular folks joining the fight.”

Since her win in the Democratic primary earlier this year, Nixon has garnered support from several lawmakers, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who campaigned with her last week, as she takes on her GOP opponent, Sen, Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), who was appointed to Marco Rubio’s seat when he became Secretary of State.

In the video shared by Jolly in his post, Obama called the former Republican congressman turned Democrat “independent-minded” and said he is “focused on lowering the cost of housing and healthcare and making sure every child gets a great education.”

“Elections are about who will fight for you and in this election, it’s David Jolly,” he added. “So, let’s do this Florida. Vote for the change you deserve.”

In his post, Jolly said he is honored to have Obama’s support.

Jolly served one term in the House as a Republican before becoming an independent in 2019. He registered as a Democrat last year and launched his gubernatorial bid. Jolly will face off against Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) in November.

data.title: China urges US Treasury to stop proposed restrictions on tech investments
data.description:
Chinese officials called on the U.S. Saturday to reconsider its proposed rule seeking to further restrict American investments into its tech industry, saying the move would disrupt trade relations between the two countries.

On Thursday, the Treasury Department proposed a rule expanding existing restrictions in the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) on hypersonic systems, quantum information technologies, high-performance computing, supercomputing and AI. The proposed mandate seeks to prevent a handful of foreign adversaries — China, Russia and North Korea — from using money from the U.S. to bolster its own technological advancement.

Beijing’s commerce ministry firmly opposed the proposal in a statement published in the Chinese Global Times, a state run media outlet, in which a spokesperson said the rule “discriminatorily” widened China-related investment restrictions.

“This is a typical case of overstretching the concept of national security. China will closely monitor subsequent developments and reserves the right to take corresponding measures,” the spokesperson said.

The ministry also said the proposal would damage ⁠economic ties between the two countries, and it reserved the right to take unspecified ​countermeasures.

The new rule also adds the biotechnology industry to the list of sectors it plans to target under OISP, an addition Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for, according to a Thursday press release from the department.

“The proposed regulations would strengthen the existing Outbound Investment Security Program to prevent our adversaries from using U.S. investment to develop critical technologies that threaten U.S. national security,” Bessent said.

The proposal will go through a public comment period before the Treasury issues a final rule.

Earlier this week, the State Department announced sanctions against five Chinese companies connected to a former Google engineer, Linwei Ding, who was convicted earlier this year of stealing AI-related trade secrets. China opposed the sanctions, saying the punishment “severely harms the legitimate rights and interests” of Chinese businesses.

data.title: Trump's former campaign manager on GOP ahead of midterms: 'It's ugly'
data.description:
President Trump’s former campaign manager is joining a growing list predicting midterm doom for Republicans, highlighting recent allegations of government corruption as a key reason.

Bill Stepien, who managed Trump’s 2020 campaign and had a stint as White House political director in the president’s first term, told CNN’s Abby Phillip that recent scandals in the administration — namely the ouster of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle — have contributed to the GOP’s poor showing in most polls.

“We talked a lot about draining the swamp 10 years ago. People wonder what’s changed when they see headlines like Guilfoyle and the trappings and the text messages,” Stepien said. “It’s ugly, and it’s given Democrats an opening.”

Guilfoyle resigned after a series of reports in The Wall Street Journal alleging she asked a GOP donor to help pay her $100,000 credit card bill ahead of her confirmation hearing.

Recent polling shows corruption is a growing issue for Americans heading into the midterms, nearing the importance of cost of living or the economy in some surveys.

Phillip cited a CNBC survey showing 36 percent of registered voters listed government corruption as the most important issue facing the country — higher than the cost of food and groceries.

A Fox News poll found that 90 percent of voters were either extremely or very concerned about government corruption, ahead of those who said the same about inflation and high prices.

The grim mood is contributing to a worsening midterm environment for Republicans, who now trail Democrats on the generic ballot by an average of 7.9 points, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s partner.

The president is attempting to boost his party by making big promises out on the campaign trail. Earlier this fall, he promised $5,000 to every voter if Republicans held control of Congress.

Trump told voters in North Carolina that Camp Lejeune toxic water settlements would be on the way, but only if the GOP wins.

“If we don’t win, there’s no money,” he said at a rally in Greenville, N.C. “If we do win, you’re getting it.”

He also tied disaster relief funds in a handful of states to Republican victories.

Overall, DDHQ’s forecast favors Democrats in the House with a 79 percent chance to flip the chamber, and narrowly favors them in the Senate, with a narrower 57 percent chance of control.

data.title: El-Sayed spats with Baier over Muslim Brotherhood question: 'Be a journalist'
data.description:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed pushed back at Fox News’s Bret Baier in an interview that aired on Friday evening over questions about his alleged ties to an Islamist political group. 

After Baier began asking the candidate about accusations repeatedly made by his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), that the Democrat has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, El-Sayed cut him off. 

“Let me just stop you right there,” the Democrat said. “You are asking this question to raise a question about whether or not I have dual loyalty.”

The journalist replied, “I’m not,” and returned to reading the campaign’s accusations. 

El-Sayed interrupted him again and accused Baier of trying to take things “out of context” and asked him to “be a journalist.”

“As a journalist, if you’re asking about my allegiance to the constitution, I have never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, I never will be a member of the Muslim Brotherhood,” El-Sayed said. 

“I’m interested in serving the United States,” he continued. “I’m interested in swearing an oath to the constitution that every senator has sworn an oath to.”

In an appearance on Fox News’s “Special Report with Bret Baier” after the interview with El-Sayed aired, Rogers repeated his claim that El-Sayed “has adopted the ideology of the Muslim Brotherhood.”

El-Sayed would be the first Muslim senator if he wins Michigan’s open Senate race. He has faced numerous attacks on the campaign trail about his family background and faith, including past comments made by his mother and half-sister. 

Rogers and other Republicans have pointed to a 2012 open letter signed on to by the Michigan Democrat to then newly elected Egyptian president, Mohamed Morsi, whose political party represented the Muslim Brotherhood’s political wing.

The letter’s signatories urged Morsi “to purge the media and police as quickly as possible.”

El-Sayed’s campaign has repeatedly denied that the Democrat has any connection to the Muslim Brotherhood, and he has publicly disavowed the group.

President Trump notably designated Lebanese, Jordanian and Egyptian chapters of the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist organizations in the U.S.

data.title: John Coale is exactly who we need to bring home our Americans
data.description:
John Coale is President Trump’s new nominee for Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs — and he is exactly the master dealmaker the job demands. With innocent Americans still languishing in prison cells in Iran, Russia, China and Afghanistan, the Senate must confirm him without delay. Lives are hanging in the balance, and Coale has already proven he knows how to break the diplomatic gridlock.

Coale masterminded the deal that used sanction relief and economic incentives to secure the release of hundreds of prisoners, including numerous American and allied citizens, from Belarus. Using such tools to free American hostages and wrongful detainees is not new, yet American diplomats, paralyzed by the lack of moral equivalence in hostage negotiations, hesitate to dip into that toolbox. Deals that could — and should — be made to bring Americans home are left on the table, forcing wrongful detainees to suffer in foreign cells far longer than they should. The irony of it all is that the deals never get better. We ultimately end up using these exact same tools — trades, sanction relief or economic incentives — to secure their release anyway.

I understand this better than anyone. My brother, an American citizen, was wrongfully detained in Iran in 2018. By 2021, a potential deal was on the table to secure his freedom and that of four other Americans through a prisoner trade and a transfer of frozen funds under strict financial oversight. It was the exact same framework that ultimately brought him home in 2023. Same deal, but with two more painful years needlessly lost behind the walls of the notorious Evin prison.

This is why the selection of John Coale, a lawyer who has viewed negotiations as a win-loss concept, is appropriate. Bound by fiduciary duty, his only focus is serving his client. In this case, that client is Trump. With innocent American lives at stake, his responsibility aligns with a cause Trump is deeply committed to protecting.

If his deal with Belarus to secure the release of hundreds of detainees is any indication, Coale will approach his role as envoy with a zero-sum mentality. We can either be pollyannish about hostage negotiations and let innocent Americans wither and die in foreign jail cells, or we can use all available tools, like Coale has shown us he is willing to, to bring them home. Ultimately, the empty prison cells in Minsk prove that transactional realism works.

By prioritizing results over rigid ideology, Coale has laid down a new blueprint for American statecraft — one that remembers the state’s most fundamental duty is to bring its people back home.

Neda Sharghi is the sister of Emad Shargi, an American citizen who was wrongfully detained in Iran from 2018 to 2023. She also serves on the Board of Directors for the James W. Foley Legacy Foundation, a nonprofit organization that advocates for American hostages and wrongful detainees.

data.title: America's next great addiction crisis
data.description:
America has a gambling problem, and it’s becoming harder to see. For decades, addiction was associated with the obvious vices: drugs, alcohol and, to a lesser extent, the desperate soul sitting at a casino table.

Today, gambling can happen anywhere, at any hour, with nothing more than a phone and a bank account. You can gamble throughout an entire football game without ever leaving the sofa. And you can lose thousands of dollars without a friend or family member even knowing.

That makes gambling addiction particularly dangerous. The addict doesn’t have to look like an addict. He can be sober and successful. He can be surrounded by people he loves while privately chasing losses on his phone. Unlike drugs or booze, gambling offers its own seductive promise of salvation. After losing a month’s salary, a gambler can convince himself that one more bet will make everything all right. Instead, one loss becomes another, and another.

Now AI threatens to make this problem many times worse. Gambling companies already collect enormous amounts of information about how customers bet, when they bet and how much they lose. AI can turn that information into a detailed picture of who is most likely to keep gambling and who is most likely to lose heavily.

The troubling question is what happens when the technology becomes better at identifying a gambler’s weaknesses than the gambler is himself.

America spent decades learning to spot a ruined life. People looked for slurred speech, bloodshot eyes, needle-marks, empty vodka bottles hidden in the laundry basket or a missing wedding ring pawned for cash.

The new system, however, leaves no real physical trace. A 25-year-old financial analyst sits in a fancy conference room in Midtown Manhattan, executing a six-figure parlay on his phone between quarterly presentations. He goes home to his apartment, eats dinner with his fiancée and then loses his entire annual bonus before the fourth quarter of a Thursday night game ends.

The brick-and-mortar casino used to force a person to cross a threshold. In 1996, if a man wanted to bet his paycheck at 3 a.m., he had to put on pants, start his car and drive somewhere specific to make a terrible decision. He had to hand paper bills to a human cashier who looked him in the eyes. That journey created natural barriers. It gave the human brain a few dozen miles to ask uncomfortable questions.

The smartphone obliterated those barriers. The casino sits in the front pocket of your jeans, right next to your mother’s text messages and dozens of work emails. It stays open at a red light, at a funeral, at a child’s piano recital, and under the covers at 2:17 a.m.

Data collection turns this total access into an asymmetric war. A gambling giant like DraftKings, which in many ways functions as a tech company, doesn’t treat its millions of users as a single, uniform crowd. Every user is an individual psychological puzzle waiting for predictive modeling to solve.

The software notes that you tend to double your wager after a heartbreaking last-second field goal. It measures the precise moment you close the app in disgust, then calculates the exact dollar amount of a “bonus bet” notification required to drag you back inside ten minutes later. This brutal system is designed to identify your impulses and monetize them, over and over again.

In many ways, it’s like nothing we have seen before. A legitimate bank deploys algorithms to flag reckless spending so the customer avoids bankruptcy and continues paying interest for 30 years. A hospital uses data to catch diseases early so the patient stays alive. A sports betting platform operates under an inverted set of incentives. The most profitable customer isn’t the cautious fan who bets $10 on the Super Bowl every February. The golden goose is the user who steadily loses, loses emotionally, and has enough liquid credit to sustain those losses over a long time.

Chemical addictions eventually demand a pause. A human body can only process a finite volume of alcohol before passing out on the carpet. A cocaine binge runs up against cardiac limits and absolute exhaustion.

Gambling works differently, because the instrument of destruction doubles as the imagined tool of salvation. When a man loses $15,000 in a night, his panicked brain doesn’t view the sportsbook app as the poison but as the only available medicine capable of producing $15,000 before sunrise. The destruction feeds the desire to do it all over again.

Traditional gambling required patience. You picked a team, placed a bet, and then waited a few hours to see who won the game. Modern micro-betting turns a contest into hundreds of tiny, high-velocity dopamine hits. You can bet on whether the next pitch in a baseball game will be a strike, whether a basketball team will make its next free throw, whether a soccer player will commit a foul before halftime, or whether a fight will break out in a hockey game within the next five minutes.

The experience feels less like sports fandom and more like a psychotic slot machine.

A recovering alcoholic doesn’t receive personalized push notifications from the local liquor store offering a free bottle of bourbon if he walks through the door before midnight. A former heroin user doesn’t open his email inbox to find a customized message offering a 20 percent discount on his next purchase because the dealer noticed he hasn’t bought anything in three weeks.

Sportsbook platforms do this continuously. With the help of AI, one should expect predation to become even more pronounced.

America has deregulated a multi-billion-dollar parasitic industry and handed it the most advanced system of psychological manipulation in human history. The consequences could be financially and socially ruinous.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

data.title: NFL forced to close 'NFL House' pop-up due to Paris protests
data.description:
The NFL closed its fan zone in Paris Saturday due to intense street protests, but the New Orleans Saints and Pittsburgh Steelers are still set to play the league’s first game in France Sunday, despite President Trump suggesting it push the face-off back.

Fans received a notification through the NFL’s “OnePass” app that the “NFL House” would be closed, citing “accessibility issues,” according to The Associated Press. The Saints similarly announced in a Saturday morning post to social platform X its fan event in Paris had been rescheduled to the following day.

Trump told reporters outside the White House Friday the NFL “probably could have postponed,” saying it looked like Saturday “is going to be a bad day in France.”

“I would’ve said the NFL could’ve probably postponed that match,” the president said. “France is really in trouble. That’s what happens when you go left.”

The president’s statement seemingly contradicted Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s Wednesday comments that U.S. officials felt it would be “fine” to hold the game. The State Department has issued a security alert for Americans traveling in the country.

“Violence and rioting have recently occurred in France and may continue. Avoid demonstrations and areas of unrest.  Stay away from areas with large crowds or significant police activity,” the department’s alert reads.

Paris, alongside other cities in France, have been rocked by demonstrations from young people, angry with the government over the state of the education system and the cost of living.

The Steelers and Saints still plan to kick off Sunday at 9:30 a.m. EDT in Stade de France. The game, one of nine NFL matches being played abroad this season, is part of an effort by the league to spread football internationally.
